The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. items.content: ICML 2027 Call For Papers The 44th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2027) will be held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, July 31-August 6 , as an in-person event. In addition to the main conference sessions, the conference will include tutorials, workshops and an expo. We invite submissions of papers on original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community for the main conference proceedings. All papers will be reviewed in a double-blind process and accepted papers will be presented at the conference. Papers must be prepared and submitted as a single file: 8 pages for the main paper, with unlimited pages for references, the impact statement, and appendices. There will be no separate deadline for the submission of supplementary material. The final versions of accepted papers will be allowed one extra page for the main paper. Note: ICML is planning to make some updates to the submission process (but not the submission format). We will announce them by late November, please stay tuned. Change in policy: two-stage reviewing process: ICML 2027 will review submissions in two stages. In the first stage, the area chair assigned to each paper decides whether it should proceed to the second stage. Papers that would clearly not be accepted receive a first-stage rejection. Every proposed first-stage reject must be confirmed by a senior area chair, and when in doubt, papers go to full review. Authors of papers that receive a first-stage rejection will be notified by February 23, 2027 with a short justification. All other papers go through the usual review process, and final decisions will be announced on May 3, 2027. This process is similar to the expedited initial review used by many top journals, where an editor or senior reviewer assesses whether a submission is sufficiently competitive to warrant a full round of external review. We recognize that any early-stage review process carries some risk that a good paper could be rejected prematurely. The requirement that every first-stage rejection be reviewed by both an AC and an SAC, together with the principle that papers should proceed to full review whenever there is doubt, is intended to minimize this risk. The goal of this process is to reduce the number of low-quality papers that go through full review. Change in policy: contribution type in submission/reviewing: ICML 2027 asks all authors to select the Contribution Type that best reflects the primary scientific contribution of their submission. The available types are General (most papers) , Theory , Application-driven , Concept and Feasibility , Negative Results , Datasets, Evaluations and Benchmarks, and Position papers. Contribution types were introduced at NeurIPS 2026. They will be used to help guide reviewing and as one factor in reviewer and Area Chair matching. Authors should select the type that best represents the main contribution of the paper, recognizing that submissions may naturally contain elements of multiple types. Please see the full ICML 2027 Contribution Types Policy and Guidance for detailed descriptions and reviewing expectations. Change in policy: LLM use in Reviewing: ICML 2027 will use a single policy for LLM use in reviewing, corresponding to Policy B of ICML 2026. In short, reviewers may use privacy-compliant LLMs to help understand the paper and related works and to polish their reviews. Delegating judgement and critique of the paper to LLMs is not allowed, and reviewers remain fully responsible for the content of their reviews. A single policy simplifies reviewer assignment and activities permitted under policy B have broad support even among authors/reviewers that chose policy A at ICML 2026 (see the paper ). The findings from ICML 2026 also suggest that effect of policy B on paper outcomes is minimal. Details and precise guidance for the reviewers are given on the LLM policy page . Change in policy: Use of Generative AI by Authors & Disclosure Policy ICML 2027 requires authors to disclose substantive use of generative AI tools in conducting the research or preparing the submission. This includes uses such as research ideation, mathematical reasoning, experimental design, code generation, data analysis, literature synthesis, and substantial manuscript drafting. Routine editorial assistance, such as spelling, grammar, formatting, and minor clarity edits, does not require disclosure. All submissions must include an AI Disclosure Statement. The statement does not count toward the paper page limit. Authors remain fully responsible for the correctness, originality, and integrity of all submitted content, including any material produced with AI assistance. When generative AI is part of the research methodology itself, its use must also be described in the paper with sufficient detail to understand and reproduce the work. Please see the full ICML 2027 Policy on the Use of Generative AI by Authors for requirements, examples, and guidance. Change in policy: Submission caps and reciprocal reviewing policy. Similar to ICLR 2027, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens reciprocal reviewing to cope with the growth in submissions. No author may appear on more than 20 submissions. Each submission must designate one of its authors as reciprocal reviewer, and an author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Each author may appear on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer. Authors with 3 or more submissions must also serve on the program committee, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. This also means that since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions. Submissions that do not meet these requirements will be desk rejected. Eligibility criteria and further details are given in the guide on Submission Quotas and Reciprocal Reviewing . Please review Author Instructions , an Example Paper , and use the correct Style Files . Submitted papers that do not conform to these policies will be rejected without review. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): general machine learning (active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis, etc.) deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.) evaluation (methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop, etc.) theory of machine learning (statistical learning theory, bandits, game theory, decision theory, etc.) machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.) optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) probabilistic methods (Bayesian methods, graphical models, Monte Carlo methods, etc.) reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.) trustworthy machine learning (reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety, etc.) application-driven machine learning (innovative techniques, problems, and datasets that are of interest to the machine learning community and driven by the needs of end-users in applications such as healthcare, physical sciences, biosciences, social sciences, sustainability, and climate etc.) Similar to last year, we also invite submissions of position papers (see the call for paper ). This year, we adopt a simplified procedure: Position papers are submitted through the main track by selecting “Position Paper” as the Contribution Type. Papers published at ICML are indexed in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research through the Journal of Machine Learning Research. We are recruiting reviewers: if you would like to volonteer, please fill this form: Self-nomination form for reviewing Important Dates and Submission Site Submission site opens: January 8, 2027. Suggested OpenReview account creation deadline: January 8, 2027. (If you do not already have an OpenReview account, please register by this date, otherwise we cannot guarantee that your account will be activated in time.**) Abstract submission deadline: January 14, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Full paper submission deadline: January 22, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Abstracts and papers can be submitted through OpenReview: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICML.cc/2027/Conference ** OpenReview: All authors must have an OpenReview account. It is strongly recommended that you sign up for OpenReview (or associate your existing account) with an institutional email. If you sign up for OpenReview with an institutional email, your account will be activated immediately; otherwise it can take up to two weeks for your account to be activated. Policies Optional in-Person Attendance Attendance for authors of accepted papers is optional. After acceptance notifications, the authors will be able to decide by a specified date whether they wish to present their paper in person at the conference or they just wish to include their paper in the proceedings (without presentation at the conference). Regardless of this choice, all the accepted papers will receive equivalent treatment in the proceedings. They will all be eligible for ICML awards as well as for the designations of distinction corresponding to the past “oral presentations” and “spotlight posters.” For proceedings-only papers, at least one of the authors must obtain virtual registration. Deadlines Abstract and paper submission deadlines are strict. In no circumstances will extensions be given. Changes to Abstract/Title/Authorship Authors should include a full title for their paper, complete author list, and complete abstract in the submission form by the abstract submission deadline. While it is possible to edit the title and abstract until the full paper submission deadline, submissions with “placeholder” abstracts that are substantially rewritten for the full submission risk being removed without consideration. The author list cannot be changed after the abstract deadline. After the abstract deadline, authors may be reordered, but not added or removed. Double-Blind Review All submissions must be anonymized and may not contain any information with the intention or consequence of violating the double-blind reviewing policy. Authors are allowed to post versions of their work on preprint servers such as arXiv. They are also allowed to give talks on the work(s) submitted to ICML during the review. However, under no circumstances should the work be advertised as an ICML submission at any time during the review period, i.e., from the time the authors submit the paper to the communication of the accept/reject decisions. If the authors have posted or plan to post a non-anonymized version of the paper online before the ICML decisions are made, the submitted version must not refer to the non-anonymized version. Dual and Concurrent Submission Authors may not submit papers that are identical, or substantially similar, to versions that have been previously published, accepted for publication, or submitted in parallel to other conferences or journals. Such submissions violate our dual submission policy, and the organizers have the right to reject such submissions, or to remove them from the proceedings. Any concurrent ICML submissions with an overlapping set of authors will also be treated as prior work (so, for example, if publishing one would render the other too incremental, then this may be considered grounds for rejection). Note that submissions that have been or are being presented at workshops without published proceedings do not violate the dual-submission policy. Reviewing Criteria Submissions should report original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community. All claims must be clearly stated and supported by reproducible experiments and/or sound theoretical analysis. The contributions must be situated in the context of the broader scientific and machine learning research literature, acknowledging and differentiating from relevant prior works as appropriate. See Reviewer Instructions for more information. Ethical Conduct for Peer Review Authors are expected to follow standard ethical conduct for peer review. In particular: Plagiarism in any form is forbidden. Prompt injection is forbidden. Advertising work (e.g., in a talk, on social media) as being under submission to ICML during the review period is forbidden. Any form of collusion, whether explicit or tacit (e.g., where authors cooperate with reviewers, ACs, or SACs to obtain favorable or unfavorable reviews) is forbidden. If you believe someone may be engaging in unethical conduct, please notify ICML by filling out the Ethics Violation Reporting form . You can also report suspected violations to program-chairs@icml.cc . All suspected unethical behaviors will be investigated by program chairs, integrity chair, or the ICML Oversight Committee, and individuals found violating the rules may face sanctions and/or have their submissions rejected. We will also collect names of individuals who are found to have violated ethics standards; if individuals representing conferences, journals, or other organizations request this list for decision-making purposes, we may make this information available to them. See Peer-review Ethics for additional details. Impact Statements Authors are required to include a statement of the potential broader impact of their work, including its ethical aspects and future societal consequences. This statement should be in a separate section at the end of the paper (co-located with Acknowledgements, before References), and does not count toward the paper page limit. In many cases, where the ethical impacts and expected societal implications are those that are well established when advancing the field of machine learning, substantial discussion is not required, and a simple statement such as: “This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.” The above statement can be used verbatim in such cases, but we encourage authors to think about whether there is content that does warrant further discussion, as this statement will be apparent if the paper is later flagged for ethics review. In particular, Reviewers and ACs may flag submissions for ethics review. Flagged submissions will be sent to an ethics review committee for comments. Ethics reviewers do not have the authority to reject papers, but in extreme cases, papers may be rejected by the program chairs on ethical grounds, regardless of scientific quality or contribution. For tips on writing the impact statement, see this post written for NeurIPS 2020 . Lay Summaries Authors of accepted papers will be required to submit a short “lay summary” of their work (also called "plain language summary") in OpenReview when submitting their camera-ready paper. As machine learning is becoming a more prevalent topic of interest in society, it is important to participate in science communication with the public. See this paper for guidelines. Additional details and examples will be provided prior to the camera-ready deadline. Self-Rankings Continuing the practice introduced at ICML 2026, authors with multiple submissions will be required to provide a self-assessment of the quality of their own submissions through a ranking. Disagreements between author rankings and reviewer scores will be used to flag papers that may warrant additional attention from area chairs and to help guide the assignment of emergency reviewers. Submitted self-rankings will be accessible only to the program chairs, associate program chairs, and integrity chairs. Area chairs will have access only to a coarse measure of disagreement between author rankings and reviewer scores. # Nov. 13th: initial version # Nov. 17h: clarification added "Since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions." # Nov. 20th: call for position papers is out. Added position paper as contribution type.

items.summary: ICML 2027 Position Papers We invite the submission of position papers to be published at the ICML 2027 conference. Position papers make an argument for a viewpoint or perspective about what should be done, in contrast to main track papers, which report on advances that have already been accomplished. Position papers also generally adopt a meta-level perspective on the field of machine learning, with wider scope than any individual area. The review criteria for position papers differs from those of the main track. Submissions to the main ICML conference track emphasize original research and novel results. In contrast, submissions to the position paper track will be judged primarily on whether they present a compelling position that warrants greater exposure within the machine learning community (regardless of whether a reviewer agrees with the position). The goal of this track is to highlight papers that stimulate constructive, civil discussion on timely topics that need our community’s

The goal of this track is to highlight papers that stimulate constructive, civil discussion on timely topics that need our community’s attention. Controversial topics are welcome. Position papers should meet standard ICML expectations for scholarship, including the use of evidence and reasoning to support all claims, inclusion of relevant background and context, and the attribution of others’ work via appropriate citations. To constitute a proper scientific contribution, a position must be non-obvious, falsifiable and defendable against credible alternatives. We discourage technical papers that have a minor persuasive element, as well as nontechnical papers that promote unsupported opinion. Accepted position papers will be presented at the conference (as oral talks or posters) and included in the conference proceedings. We want to hear your positions. What is the field getting right? Getting wrong? Position papers may address any aspect relevant to machine learning (ML), including but not limited to: Concerns about data legality, copyright, and intellectual property in ML The role of privacy in ML training and deployment The role of open-source versus closed-source ML models for research Regulation of ML technology (licensing, evaluation, disclosures, post-deployment monitoring, etc.) Ethical considerations when conducting ML research and deploying ML systems User guidance for responsible use of ML tools, services, applications, etc. What the next generation of ML researchers needs to know How we can improve the beneficial impact of our community’s work We encourage you to browse the position papers that were published at ICML 2026 for examples (and ideas to build on, or from which to offer an alternative position). The paper must include an “Alternative Views” section in the main body of the paper (not an appendix) that describes and addresses one or more credible (not strawmen) positions that are opposed to the paper’s position. The following are not required for position papers: Impact Statements (the position paper itself should explain the impact) Lay Summaries (the position paper itself should be accessible to the public) The reciprocal reviewing requirement The self-ranking requirement. We encourage the inclusion of a "Call to Action" section that identifies plausible steps to realizing the aims of the stated position. By the end of the paper the reader should know what steps should be taken by whom to bring about these desired outcomes. Position: The paper clearly states a position on machine learning, see example aspects listed earlier in this CFP. Papers that describe technical research without advocating a position are not responsive to this call and should instead be submitted to the main paper track. Support: The paper supports its position with clear reasoning and evidence where appropriate. Significance: The paper demonstrates that the position is important, in terms of scope, impact, timeliness, risks, benefits, etc. Discussion potential: The position is likely to inspire constructive, civil discussion within the ICML community. The reviewer need not agree with the stated position. Alternative views: The paper describes and addresses one or more credible (not strawmen) positions that are opposed to the paper’s position. Call to Action: The paper identifies plausible steps to realizing the aims of the stated position. By the end of the paper the reader should know what steps should be taken by whom to bring about these desired outcomes. Communication quality: The paper is well organized and clearly written. Context: The paper includes a discussion of (and citations to) literature and events relevant to the stated position. Questions? items.content: Eight EU countries join forces to develop trusted, accessible digital education services and strengthen digital sovereignty. © European Commission Eight EU Member States have established the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) to develop shared digital infrastructure and services for schools, teachers and learners across Europe. The consortium brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Spain, with its statutory seat in The Hague, Netherlands. Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education and Equality of the Netherlands, said: “The use of digital teaching resources, AI-supported reviewing of schoolwork and other new software within the classroom: digital innovations develop rapidly and prove tough to keep up with. But schools should always be able to count on the safety and availability of the systems that are being used in the classroom. With this unique European cooperation, we can tackle these issues together and lay the foundation for developing digital applications in a responsible manner. This way, we support our teachers and students and help schools within the European Union to digitally stand on their own feet. I am proud The Netherlands takes a leading role in this.” Established by a European Commission decision on 4 November 2026 , the EDU-EDIC provides a framework for Member States to pool resources, share expertise and jointly develop digital education solutions. Its objective is to strengthen Europe's technological sovereignty in education while making trusted and accessible digital tools more widely available to pupils and teachers. Developing shared digital infrastructure Digital education systems increasingly rely on technologies and services developed by providers outside the EU. At the same time, differences between national systems can make it difficult to share resources, exchange data securely or deploy common solutions. The EDU-EDIC aims to address these challenges through cooperation between Member States. Its activities will focus on: Digital infrastructures: developing a trusted, interoperable and sovereign European digital education ecosystem through common technical standards, shared governance frameworks and secure digital infrastructures that enable cross-border connectivity and cooperation. Data: establishing a trusted and interoperable European framework for educational data through common data standards, governance arrangements and secure data exchange mechanisms that enable data portability, responsible reuse and cross-sector collaboration. Artificial intelligence (AI): supporting learners and educators by fostering the development, adoption and scaling of trustworthy, responsible and effective European AI-powered educational solutions that boosts teaching, learning and educational innovation. Support for EdTech and other educational solution providers: supporting the European educational technology (EdTech) ecosystem, mostly composed by SMEs and micro-enterprises, and fostering trusted collaboration among public authorities, educational institutions, research organisations, technology providers, open-source communities and other relevant stakeholders to support the development, adoption and scaling of innovative educational solutions. EDU-EDIC aims at providing shared infrastructure and services that participating countries can use according to common rules and to their needs. Making digital education more accessible A central ambition of the EDU-EDIC is to make digital technologies more accessible to schools, teachers and learners across the Union. By sharing infrastructure, investments and expertise, Member States can reduce duplication and improve access to digital solutions that might otherwise be difficult or costly to develop individually. This approach can help narrow the digital divide between education systems and support more equal opportunities for learners across Europe. The consortium will also promote solutions that reflect European values, including equality, accessibility, privacy and the protection of personal data. These principles are particularly important in education, where digital technologies must respond to the needs of learners and educators while providing a safe and trusted environment. Strengthening European cooperation The EDU-EDIC is part of the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium framework, introduced under the Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 to support multi-country digital projects. Through this framework, Member States can jointly invest in and operate digital infrastructure, while maintaining a central role in its governance. The EDU- EDIC will allow participating countries to coordinate their efforts, develop common solutions and strengthen Europe's capacity to provide its own digital education technologies. Other Member States are highly encouraged to join the EDU-EDIC, as members or observers, agreeing to the conditions set out in its statutes, opening the door to wider European cooperation on digital education. The consortium was officially launched on 20 November 2026, with the participation of European Commission Executive Vice-Presidents Henna Virkkunen and Roxana Mînzatu, and Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education and Equality of the Netherlands. Last update 20 November 2026 Print as PDF

In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. ClaudeŌĆÖs result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but theyŌĆÖre mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites themŌĆöŌĆ£quantum gravityŌĆØŌĆöis one of the fieldŌĆÖs biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because theyŌĆÖre one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matterŌĆöthey pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, ŌĆ£writtenŌĆØ on the universeŌĆÖs outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: itŌĆÖs a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100┬░C. But Hawking and PageŌĆÖs calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didnŌĆÖt know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and PageŌĆÖs, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isnŌĆÖt just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists donŌĆÖt know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldnŌĆÖt prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesnŌĆÖt identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about ClaudeŌĆÖs methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing ClaudeŌĆÖs capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each otherŌĆÖs progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that HongbinŌĆÖs agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another oneŌĆöwhich was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional spaceŌĆöturned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling canŌĆÖt be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that youŌĆÖre heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, thatŌĆÖs not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. ItŌĆÖs an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but itŌĆÖs also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the ŌĆ£sum over histories,ŌĆØ is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and PageŌĆÖs work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine youŌĆÖre standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isnŌĆÖt like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a ŌĆ£historyŌĆØ means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particlesŌĆöincluding gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observeŌĆöit ŌĆ£wins.ŌĆØ At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperatureŌĆöwhich physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperatureŌĆöthe universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. ItŌĆÖs a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. ThatŌĆÖs very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ŌĆÖt Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in generalŌĆöthat everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universeŌĆÖs outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introductionŌĆötheyŌĆÖre two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. ItŌĆÖs related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and PageŌĆÖs gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and PageŌĆÖs findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and PageŌĆÖs, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles donŌĆÖt interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagramsŌĆöfar too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasnŌĆÖt the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong couplingŌĆöthe blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100┬░C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please donŌĆÖt do this; itŌĆÖs dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditionsŌĆöif the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or chargeŌĆöthen some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. The modular bootstrap As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: itŌĆÖs called ŌĆ£3D gravityŌĆØ because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowlŌĆÖs rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. ItŌĆÖs also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isnŌĆÖt a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scalesŌĆöthe Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignoreŌĆöblack holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. ClaudeŌĆÖs results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesnŌĆÖt try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isnŌĆÖt even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. HereŌĆÖs how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, MŌéü, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and MŌéü, and look for inconsistencies. To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shapeŌĆöthe dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is ŌĆ£written,ŌĆØ in one fewer dimension. Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is ŌĆ£writtenŌĆØ on its surface. The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus . There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call ŌĆ£timeŌĆØ and which we call ŌĆ£space.ŌĆØ In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, theyŌĆÖre swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time. Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop. In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it canŌĆÖt matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment. Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesnŌĆÖt matter which

To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and PageŌĆÖs work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine youŌĆÖre standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isnŌĆÖt like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a ŌĆ£historyŌĆØ means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particlesŌĆöincluding gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observeŌĆöit ŌĆ£wins.ŌĆØ At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperatureŌĆöwhich physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperatureŌĆöthe universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. ItŌĆÖs a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. ThatŌĆÖs very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ŌĆÖt Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in generalŌĆöthat everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universeŌĆÖs outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introductionŌĆötheyŌĆÖre two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. ItŌĆÖs related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and PageŌĆÖs gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and PageŌĆÖs findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and PageŌĆÖs, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles donŌĆÖt interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagramsŌĆöfar too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasnŌĆÖt the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong couplingŌĆöthe blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100┬░C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please donŌĆÖt do this; itŌĆÖs dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditionsŌĆöif the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or chargeŌĆöthen some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowlŌĆÖs rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. ItŌĆÖs also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isnŌĆÖt a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scalesŌĆöthe Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignoreŌĆöblack holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. ClaudeŌĆÖs results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesnŌĆÖt try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isnŌĆÖt even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. HereŌĆÖs how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, MŌéü, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and MŌéü, and look for inconsistencies. To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shapeŌĆöthe dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is ŌĆ£written,ŌĆØ in one fewer dimension. Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is ŌĆ£writtenŌĆØ on its surface. The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus . In the second, theyŌĆÖre swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time. Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop. In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. items.title: European Digital Infrastructure Consortium launches today to strengthen digital sovereignty in education
items.summary: Today, the European Commission and eight Member States are launching the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) to pool resources and develop shared, secure and interoperable digital infrastructure and services for education. GettyImages © anyaberkut The new consortium on education brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands, which will be hosting the EDIC. The initiative will strengthen Europe's technological resilience while making high-quality digital tools accessible to schools, teachers and learners. It will also help narrow the digital divide in education by supporting solutions that can be used across national education systems, regardless of their resources or technological capacity. Today's launch marks an important milestone in fostering innovation and excellence in education and contributing to the EU's technological sovereignty ambitions. items.content: Today, the European Commission and eight Member States are launching the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) to pool resources and develop shared, secure and interoperable digital infrastructure and services for education. GettyImages © anyaberkut The new consortium on education brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands, which will be hosting the EDIC. The initiative will strengthen Europe's technological resilience while making high-quality digital tools accessible to schools, teachers and learners. It will also help narrow the digital divide in education by supporting solutions that can be used across national education systems, regardless of their resources or technological capacity. Today's launch marks an important milestone in fostering innovation and excellence in education and contributing to the EU's technological sovereignty ambitions. Executive Vice-Presidents Henna Virkkunen and Roxana Mînzatu, together with Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education of the Netherlands, will welcome the launch. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: “Today's launch of the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education is an important step towards achieving Europe's technological sovereignty in one of our most sensitive and strategic sectors. Education shapes our future, and Europe must be able to rely on trusted, safe and interoperable digital solutions that reflect European values and principles. By working together with the Member States, we can build a resilient European digital education infrastructure that supports learners, educators and schools across the Union.” Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness, said: “Recently, we officially launched the Education and Skills Package and announced the establishment of the EDU-EDIC consortium. Today, we are reiterating our commitment to reinforce education for Europe's future. Our priority is to ensure that education is ready for the AI era. We will work together with Member States to pool expertise in strategic areas such as cloud infrastructure, AI for education, secure data exchange across educational institutions, and Europe's education technology (EdTech) sector.” You can also read more about other European Digital Infrastructure Consortium (EDIC) . Related content News article 20 November 2026 Member States join forces to develop sovereign digital infrastructure on education Eight EU countries join forces to develop trusted, accessible digital education services and strengthen digital sovereignty. Last update 20 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.content: The second meeting of the AI Act Advisory Forum took place, in hybrid format, on Monday 16 November in Brussels. ©AdobeStock Nataliya One of the highlights of the meeting was the election of the two co-Chairs. Mrs Laura Lázaro Cabrera and Mrs Catarina Nunes Santos were elected. Both co-Chairs have taken on the responsibility of leading the Forum and representing its views for the next two years. Mrs Laura Lázaro Cabrera, representing the non-commercial views of the Forum, is Director of the Equity and Data programme and Deputy Director and Counsel to the Center for Democracy and Technology (CDT) Europe in Brussels, where she leads the work promoting the effective protection of fundamental human rights in the implementation of European Union legislation regulating new technologies. Mrs Catarina Santos Nunes, representing the commercial views of the Forum, is the Chief Operating Officer and Chief Compliance Office at Starkdata. Starkdata is a Portuguese company and provides an AI-powered predictive analytics platform which enables businesses to make data-driven decisions. Forum members adopted the Forum's Rule of Procedure, giving the Forum a clear framework for its functioning and for its decision-making process. Items discussed The meeting was kicked off with presentations from the AI Office. Updates on the current work of the AI Office were shared, and included insights on its enforcement activities, its work on innovation, the EU KIDS Act, and the Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI. Discussions on the stocktaking on technological developments of AI, covering the latest developments in terms of AI capabilities, incidents as well as industrial application and AI R&D automation, also took place. The Chair of the AI Board , Mrs Jean Carberry, the Chair and the Vice-Chair of the Scientific Panel , Mr Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh, and Nicolas Moës, gave Advisory Forum participants information on their two respective bodies, exploring the synergies between the Advisory Forum, the AI Board and the Scientific Panel, the governance bodies established under the EU AI Act. The Advisory Forum was presented with possible work streams on which the AI Office wishes to seek its advice. Members were invited to discuss one of two topics: AI companions or AI agents, as well as the future of its work. The discussions took place in breakout groups, which subsequently reported to the plenary, sharing their main conclusions on both topics. More on the AI Act Advisory Forum Related content News article 19 June 2026 The AI Act Advisory Forum convenes its kick-off meeting On 19 June, the Commission hosted the inaugural session of the AI Act Advisory Forum, the general advisory body to the European Commission and the AI Board, supporting the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act. Last update 20 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. Trump Protects the Executive’s Privileges and Enhances Efficiencies in Federal Contracting briefings & statements Congressional Bills H.R. 5284, H.R. 8352, and H.R. 10159 Signed into Law November 20, 2026 Read more : Congressional Bills H.R. 5284, H.R. 8352, and H.R. 10159 Signed into Law presidential actions NATIONAL ADOPTION MONTH, 2026 November 20, 2026 Read more : NATIONAL ADOPTION MONTH, 2026 promises made, promises kept 01 The Trump administration made incredible strides in its effort to Make America Healthy Again, with roughly 35% of the American food industry — including major corporations like Walmart, Hershey and Nestlé — agreeing to eliminate artificial dyes from their products. 02 At President Trump’s direction, the Department of Health and Human Services revised its childhood vaccine recommendations from 72 shots for 11 diseases to 10 “consensus vaccines.” 03 President Trump established the Make America Healthy Again Commission, tasked with investigating and addressing the root causes of America’s escalating health crisis, with an initial focus on childhood chronic diseases. 04 Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins signed a slew of waivers allowing states to remove junk food from SNAP. 05 The Department of Health and Human Services removed COVID-19 vaccines from the list of shots recommended for healthy children and pregnant women. 06 Following negotiations with the Trump Administration, a variety of major pharmaceutical companies have agreed to bring American drug prices in line with the lowest paid by other developed nations, ending decades of Big Pharma exploiting U.S. consumers. 07 President Trump secured $50 billion in funding for rural hospitals. 08 President Trump signed the Whole Milk for Health Kids Act into law, restoring nutritious whole and 2% milk in American schools. 09 The Trump Administration Rollins released new dietary guidelines that prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods over processed junk. items.title: Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo
items.summary: Agentic AI / Generative AI English 中文 Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo Nov 19, 2026 By Amr Elmeleegy , Harry Kim and Kyle Kranen Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Dynamo provides a serving layer that coordinates distributed rollout generation for reinforcement learning training. KV-aware routing balances cache reuse and worker load to reduce redundant prompt computation and rollout delays. ModelExpress accelerates weight distribution by transferring compressed delta updates and reusing weights already resident in GPU memory. Recovery mechanisms detect worker failures, reroute requests to healthy capacity, and enable replacement workers to catch up using checkpoint and delta loading. Open-source integrations connect Dynamo to existing RL stacks including verl , NeMo RL, Slime, and prime-rl.
